headline: Share your DSPi on the network, and Console now updates itself
items: DSPi Link shares the DSPi plugged into this PC with phones, browsers and other Consoles on your local network. Switch it on under Settings > General > Networking. Leave access Open, or require each new client to pair with a six-digit code and choose whether it can only watch, change the sound, or administer the hub.
A browser on the same network can open this PC's address to reach a control page that Console serves itself.
Console finds DSPi devices shared by other computers and ESP32 bridges, and lists them in the device list marked with the hub they are on. Hubs can also be added by address.

Console can keep running in the notification area as a sharing hub, and can open at login. Turn this on under Settings > General > Background, or choose Minimise to Notification Area from the main menu.
Console checks for new releases and can download, verify and install them in place. Find it under Settings > Software Update, or choose Check for Updates from the Help menu.
When several Consoles watch one device's spectrum analyser, the last one to choose channels drives and the others follow it, with a Take control button, instead of overwriting each other.
Saving a preset, importing a configuration or learning an IR code holds other Consoles off the device until it finishes. A change refused that way says another console is applying changes.
Settings > General > Globals has a Latency setting. Pick a target from 0.67 ms to 8 ms. The 0.67 and 1 ms options suit S/PDIF, I2S and ADAT inputs, and run as 2 ms on USB.

Stats has an Output Ring Health section showing the fill target, underruns, the lowest fill and the worst input gaps, so you can tell whether a latency setting holds up. Buffer fill is shown in fine steps.
Give the board its own name under Settings > General > Globals, and rename its input sources there or by right-clicking the source picker. The device list and DSPi Link hubs show the names.
Control Surfaces can save the active preset and set the target latency. The Input & Presets family is now called Device, and display pages choose their parameter from a menu grouped by family.
Filter files now use the same format as DSPi Console for macOS, and importing one reports any filters it could not apply. The AutoEQ database can be rebuilt from GitHub.
The sidebar can be resized by dragging its edge, and a double-click puts it back. I2S data pins on unused pairs are listed under Unused pairs, and external mute offers hold and release times.
File > Exit now asks about unsaved changes and pending Settings, and won't quit during a firmware update, just as closing the window always did.

With firmware 1.1.6, level meters and clip indicators on the RP2040 no longer read 6 dB hot, a bypassed EQ band no longer stays bypassed after a factory reset, and outputs on a mixed S/PDIF and I2S layout no longer fall silent after playback pauses. Slave mode also tracks an S/PDIF, ADAT or I2S source more closely.

headline: Tube modelling, output limiters, a spectrum analyser and filters you shape on the graph
items: The Tube Modeller gives each output the character of one of 16 popular vacuum tubes, with drive, mix and an output stage that recreates how a valve amplifier's transformer meets a loudspeaker. Find it in the menu under Tube Modeller (Ctrl+Shift+D).

Every output now has its own brickwall limiter with adjustable threshold and release. Click the icon under an output's mute button to switch it on, or right-click it for settings. Linked outputs share their limiter settings.

A spectrum analyser shows the sound on any input or output as it plays: behind the response graph, as bars under it, and in its own window (Ctrl+Shift+A). The device does the measuring, so it works with every source, including S/PDIF, ADAT and I2S.
The Subharmonic Synthesizer adds a new octave below the bass, for recordings that are light on low end (Ctrl+Shift+S).
Filters can now be edited directly on the response graph. Drag a band's dot to change its frequency and gain, scroll to change its width, and use the card beside it to pick a shape.
Console now carries the matching firmware and installs it for you from File > Update Firmware. If a connected device runs a different version, a banner offers the update.
A setup wizard on first launch walks you through installing DSPi on a Pico. You can skip it, and run it again from Help in the menu.
Control Surfaces can now switch auxiliary outputs: a relay, lamp or amplifier trigger on a spare GPIO pin.
Dashboard cards sit in a grid that uses the width of the window. Choose Auto or one to three per row from the gear on any card.

The tool windows have been redesigned. The effect windows place their controls and graphs side by side and are gathered under Effects in the menu, and the Signal Generator, Statistics and Interrupt Monitor have been rebuilt.

Channel pages can copy and paste their settings (Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V), outputs have Clear All, and the filter type menu groups the shelves and cuts by slope. Preamp, gain and delay can be typed, and a right-click resets them to zero.

The Matrix Mixer shows gain and invert only on connected crosspoints, adds a trim to each input row along with Direct 1:1 and Clear, and gives each output a right-click menu to identify, rename, copy or paste it.

Filter files exported from DSPi Console for macOS now import correctly, and the preamp in an AutoEQ or REW file is applied with its filters. Exports keep full precision and include every channel, so importing one puts the channels back exactly as they were.

Many reliability fixes: switching between two DSPis no longer resets the new device's volume, moving quickly between filter fields or bands no longer loses an edit, unsaved changes are tracked more accurately, and the Console reconnects by itself when a connection goes stale after a quick replug or a wake from sleep.
Help in the menu has Getting Started, What's New and links to DSPi on GitHub, and Alt-click renames a channel in the sidebar.
